steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on adaptive background music for a fighting game. Explain the motivation around player experience, the competition platform we build on, why fighting games, our goal and evaluation, and our contributions.

steps.text:

  - forms: gameplay changes, visuals, music / sound effects

- BGM
  - focus: video game music to enhance experience; BGM aids immersion
  - fighting game BGM should follow dynamic action: suspense, excitement
  - usually pre-composed looping songs -> miss combat intensity
- Why fighting games

  - two-and-a-half-dimensional (left/right; some attacks/dodges leave 2D)
  - fairly simple -> larger audience
  - uses DareFightingICE

  - first on adaptive music in fighting games

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Video games keep getting more popular, and video game developers are trying to improve their games so that they leave a positive impression on players by enhancing their experience. The improvements come in many forms, like changes to gameplay, games that are visually pleasing, or games with very enjoyable music or sound effects. Whatever the type of improvement is, the final goal is to make the overall experience of the players better.

Our work is based on the DareFightingICE Competition, which has two tracks, a Sound Design Track and an AI Track. It was held at the 2022 IEEE Conference on Games (CoG 2022). The platform of the competition is DareFightingICE, which is an enhanced version of FightingICE with better sound design and a new AI interface that can give audio data to AIs.

This research is about video game music and how it can be used to enhance the players' experience. BGM helps a lot in making the gaming experience immersive. In fighting games the BGM should change with the dynamic action and create suspense and excitement while the players are fighting. But fighting game BGM is usually done with pre-composed songs that loop, and these do not capture the intensity of the combat accurately.

- Why fighting games
  - one-versus-one fights, attacks and abilities
  - two-and-a-half-dimensional; some moves leave 2D
  - simple -> larger audience; uses DareFightingICE
- Goal and contributions
  - adaptive BGM from DareFightingICE BGM; evaluated with Blind DL AI (audio only)
  - first: adaptive music in fighting games; multiple instruments; game state info via BGM

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Video games keep getting more popular, and video game developers are trying to improve their games so that they leave a positive impression on players by enhancing their experience. The improvements come in many forms, like changes to gameplay, games that are visually pleasing, or games with very enjoyable music or sound effects. Whatever the type of improvement is, the final goal is to make the overall experience of the players better.

Our work is based on the DareFightingICE Competition, which has two tracks, a Sound Design Track and an AI Track. It was held at the 2022 IEEE Conference on Games (CoG 2022). The platform of the competition is DareFightingICE, which is an enhanced version of FightingICE with better sound design and a new AI interface that can give audio data to AIs.

This research is about video game music and how it can be used to enhance the players' experience. BGM helps a lot in making the gaming experience immersive. In fighting games the BGM should change with the dynamic action and create suspense and excitement while the players are fighting. But fighting game BGM is usually done with pre-composed songs that loop, and these do not capture the intensity of the combat accurately.

So the target genre of this research is fighting games. In fighting games a player fights one-versus-one against another player or a computer player and uses different attacks and abilities to beat the opponent. These games are two-and-a-half-dimensional, which means the players can only move in two dimensions (left or right, while in some fighting games the players can do an attack or dodge that takes them out of 2D). Also, fighting games are fairly simple compared to other genres of video games, so they are open to a larger audience. This research uses DareFightingICE.

The goal of this research is to make adaptive BGM by modifying the BGM of DareFightingICE, and to evaluate how well the adaptive BGM performs using a deep learning AI that only takes audio as input (Blind DL AI). Our contributions are:

- 1. We are the first group to focus on adaptive music in fighting games.

- 2. We are also the first group to use multiple instruments when adapting a BGM.

- 3. Our research focuses on giving players information about the state of the game through the BGM.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
As video games keep growing in popularity, video game developers are trying to improve their games to leave a positive impression on players by enhancing their experience [1]. These improvements take many different forms, such as gameplay-related changes, visually pleasing games, or games with very enjoyable music or sound effects. Regardless of the type of improvement, the ultimate goal is to enhance the overall experience of the players.

Our work is based on the DareFightingICE Competition, which has two tracks: a Sound Design Track and an AI Track [2]. It ran at the 2022 IEEE Conference on Games (CoG 2022). The platform for the competition is DareFightingICE, an enhanced version of FightingICE [3] with an enhanced sound design and a new AI interface that can give audio data to AIs.

This research focuses on video game music and how to use it to enhance players' experience. BGM greatly aids an immersive gaming experience [4,5]. In fighting games, BGM should change in response to the dynamic action, creating suspense and excitement as the players engage in combat. However, fighting game BGM is typically implemented using pre-composed looping songs, which fall short of accurately capturing the intensity of combat.

As a result, the target genre of this research is fighting games. In fighting games, players fight against another player or a computer player in a one-versus-one match, using different attacks and abilities to overcome the opponent. These fighting games are two-and-a-half-dimensional, meaning that the players can only move in two dimensions (left or right, while in some fighting games the players can perform an attack or dodge that takes them out of 2D). In addition, because fighting games are fairly simple compared to other video game genres, they are open to a larger audience. This research uses DareFightingICE.

The goal of this research is to create adaptive BGM by modifying the BGM of DareFightingICE, and to evaluate the performance of the adaptive BGM using a deep learning AI that only uses audio as input (Blind DL AI) [6]. The contributions of our work are as follows:

- 1. We are the first group to focus on adaptive music in fighting games.

- 2. We are also the first group to use multiple instruments in the adaptation of a BGM.

- 3. Our research focuses on giving players information about the state of the game through the BGM.

References:
[1] B. Berg Marklund, H. Engström, M. Hellkvist, and P. Backlund, “What Empirically Based Research Tells Us About Game Development,” in The Computer Games Journal , vol. 8, no. 3-4, pp. 179–198, 2019.
[2] I. Khan, T. V. Nguyen, X. Dai, and R. Thawonmas, “DareFightingICE Competition: A Fighting Game Sound Design and AI Competition,” 2022 IEEE Conference on Games (CoG) , pp. 478–485, 2022.
[3] F. Lu, K. Yamamoto, L. H. Nomura, S. Mizuno, Y. M. Lee, and R. Thawonmas, “Fighting Game Artificial Intelligence Competition Platform,” 2013 IEEE 2nd Global Conference on Consumer Electronics (GCCE) , pp. 320–323, Oct. 2013. (https://www.ice.ci.ritsumei.ac.jp/ ftgaic/index.htm)
[4] C. Klimmt, D. Possler, N. May, H. Auge, L. Wanjek, and A.-L. Wolf, “Effects of soundtrack music on the video game experience,” in Media Psychology , vol. 22, no. 5, pp. 689–713, 2018.
[5] E. de la Mora Velasco and A. Hirumi, “The effects of background music on learning: A systematic review of literature to guide future research and practice,” Educational Technology Research and Development , vol. 68, no. 6, pp. 2817–2837, 2020.
[6] T. Van Nguyen, X. Dai, I. Khan, R. Thawonmas, and H. V. Pham, “A Deep Reinforcement Learning Blind AI in DareFightingICE,” 2022 IEEE Conference on Games (CoG) , pp. 632–637, 2022.
